question: Which change in an API is a breaking change?

options.text: Adding a new optional field to the response
options.explanation: Adding a field is a non-breaking change. Clients that don't know about the new field will simply ignore it.

options.text: Renaming an existing field
options.explanation: Renaming is a classic breaking change. All clients accessing the old field name will receive undefined instead of the value.

options.text: Adding a new optional query parameter
options.explanation: A new optional parameter does not break old clients: they simply won't use it.

options.text: Adding a new endpoint
options.explanation: A new endpoint is a non-breaking change. Existing clients don't call it and don't know about its existence.

question: A company releases a public API with 10,000 registered developers. Clients are written in various languages. Which versioning strategy is preferred?

options.text: Header versioning (Accept: vnd.api.v2+json)
options.explanation: Header versioning requires HTTP client configuration in every SDK. With 10,000 developers across different languages, this creates many failure points.

options.text: URL versioning (/v2/users)
options.explanation: URL versioning is the best choice for a large public audience. The version is visible without knowledge of the protocol, easy to test from a browser or curl, and requires no special client configuration.

options.text: Query param versioning (?version=2)
options.explanation: Query versioning is less obvious. Developers may forget to pass the parameter and get an unexpected default version.

options.text: Don't version — only make additive changes
options.explanation: Additive changes are good practice, but breaking changes are sometimes inevitable. Without a versioning strategy, you cannot make architectural changes.

question: What does the HTTP Sunset header in an API response mean?

options.text: The API only works during certain hours
options.explanation: The Sunset header has nothing to do with API scheduling. It is not about time-based availability.

options.text: The date and time when this endpoint or API version will be shut down
options.explanation: Sunset (RFC 8594) is a standard header indicating a specific shutdown date. Clients must migrate before this date.

options.text: The API is deprecated but the shutdown date is not defined
options.explanation: The Deprecation header is used to indicate deprecation without a specific date. Sunset always contains a concrete date.

options.text: The header points to the previous API version
options.explanation: The Link header with a rel attribute is used to point to another version. Sunset is only about the shutdown date.

question: Select all advantages of Header versioning:

options.text: The resource URL remains unchanged across all versions
options.explanation: Exactly. /api/users — one URL for all versions. The version is passed in request metadata, not in the resource address.

options.text: Easy to test from a browser address bar
options.explanation: This is a drawback of Header versioning. Browsers don't easily allow setting the Accept header. You need tools like Postman or curl.

options.text: Conforms to HTTP Content Negotiation principle
options.explanation: Header versioning uses the Content Negotiation mechanism from RFC 7231: the client specifies a preferred format via Accept, and the server responds accordingly.

options.text: Versions are easy to cache without additional configuration
options.explanation: This is a problem. CDNs and proxies cache by URL. Without a Vary: Accept header, the cache may return v1 to a client that requested v2.

question: API v1 was released 2 years ago. You want to shut it down. What is the minimum recommended period between deprecation notice and shutdown for a public API?

options.text: 1 week
options.explanation: One week is not enough. Development teams may be busy with other tasks, and release cycles can take months.

options.text: 1 month
options.explanation: One month is too short for a public API. Not all clients follow notifications and will have time to migrate.

options.text: 6 months or more
options.explanation: Industry practice — at least 6 months for public APIs. Major companies (Stripe, GitHub) give a year or more. This allows teams to schedule migration in their sprints.

options.text: The timeframe doesn't matter as long as you warn
options.explanation: The timeframe is critical. A simple warning without sufficient time creates problems for clients and damages the API's reputation.
